title: Age of first drinking and adult alcohol problems: Systematic review of prospective cohort studies

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether drinking at a young age causes alcohol problems in adulthood, or whether the same family, genetic and personal factors lead to both. In general-population cohorts that recorded the age of the first drink during adolescence, an earlier first drink went with more adult drinking or alcohol problems in some analyses and not in others, and the association often shrank when other risk factors were taken into account. A systematic review found only four such cohorts up to January 2013 (two in the USA and two in Norway; 447 to 1,311 people each; five reports; no meta-analysis; confidence in the review rated critically low on its study card): in an Oslo school cohort, a later first drink went with less drinking and fewer problems at 18 to 21, with control only for parents' and peers' influence; in a US community cohort, a first drink before 11 went with problem drinking by 31 (odds ratios 2.39 and 5.75, depending on where the first drink happened) but not after adjustment for further risk factors, while feeling drunk at the first drink remained a predictor; in the Young in Norway cohort, drinking by 13 to 14 went with frequent intoxication (odds ratio 1.5, 95% CI 1.2 to 1.9) and with an AUDIT score of 8 or more, a screen for risky drinking (1.6, 1.3 to 2.1), at 26 to 27, both falling to 1.2 (0.9 to 1.6) after adjustment for conduct problems in adolescence; in a Seattle cohort, the age of the first drink was not associated with adult alcohol misuse or with ever having alcohol dependence, but a first drink before 11 went with more years with dependence (odds ratio 1.68) and, in a later report, with more chronic dependence, essentially unchanged across four adjusted models. The review's abstract says that rigorous adjustment markedly weakens or removes such associations, which its own Seattle summary contradicts; the authors conclude that it is not yet known whether starting earlier leads to adult problems, and found that feeling drunk at the first drink and the start of regular drinking went with adult problems more strongly than the age of the first drink (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014). In a Minnesota cohort of twins born 1977 to 1984 (1,512 twins at about age 11; drinking reported at 14, at the time; outcomes at about 25), twins who had drunk without their parents' permission by 14 already differed beforehand, notably in delinquent behaviour and in their parents' drinking and smoking; after weighting for 29 childhood characteristics, early drinking was associated with a higher adult alcohol-use score (standardized coefficient 0.57, SE 0.06), and within twin pairs who differed in early drinking the association was about a third as large but remained (0.21, SE 0.09, in all pairs; 0.22, SE 0.10, in identical pairs, who share all their genes and their family), whereas within identical pairs early drinking was not clearly associated with symptoms of alcohol abuse or dependence (0.17, SE 0.14) (Irons et al., 2015). Twin comparisons remove what co-twins share, not differences between them such as their own early use of tobacco or other drugs. Grant & Dawson (1998), the national survey analysis of age at first drug use and drug use disorders, is not yet read. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable as a causal effect. Maimaris & McCambridge (2014), four cohorts, no pooling: Oslo (n = 522) structural coefficients −3.465 for debut age on consumption and −13.828 on a problem index (p < 0.0001), with parental and peer control only; Rutgers (n = 447) first drink before 11, OR 2.39 (95% CI 1.10–5.20) at a family gathering and 5.75 (1.53–21.54) elsewhere for lifetime problem drinking by 31, not significant in the fully adjusted model (coefficient −0.0631), feeling drunk at the first drink 0.3848 (p < 0.0001); Seattle (n = 808) no association with misuse or any dependence (ORs 0.96, 1.40 and 0.64 against a first drink at 11–14), first drink before 11 and waves with dependence OR 1.68 (p < 0.05; no intervals), later report (n = 706) chronicity β 0.44 unadjusted and 0.45 to 0.53 in four adjusted models; Young in Norway (n = 1,311) frequent intoxication OR 1.5 (1.2–1.9) and AUDIT 8 or more 1.6 (1.3–2.1), both 1.2 (0.9–1.6) after adjustment for conduct problems. Irons et al. (2015), drinking without permission by 14, standardized β (SE): adult alcohol-use index, weighted 0.57 (0.06), within all discordant pairs 0.21 (0.09), identical pairs 0.22 (0.10), fraternal pairs 0.20 (0.14); alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms, weighted 0.36, all pairs 0.24 (0.11), identical 0.17 (0.14), fraternal 0.34 (0.16); intoxication by 14 and alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms within all pairs 0.29 (0.15). The twin study's printed p-values are not used (card reporting issue).
